lesson.title: Decisions
lesson.driving_question: How can a program choose between two recommendations?
lesson.primary_concept_family: A Boolean condition chooses one of two indented code blocks.
misconceptions: A condition uses == to compare values; = assigns a value.
The indented block belongs to the if or else line above it.
Only one branch of an if/else statement runs.
The else block runs when the if condition is false.
representation_coverage: translation between a two-way flow diagram and if/else code

progression.retrieve: read an input and display a value
progression.modify_b: add a name to both branches
progression.make: write a new two-outcome drink recommendation

code_expectations: Use a colon after if and else.
Indent each branch by four spaces.
Keep the two outcomes visibly different.

Without running the code, use the exact input 'walk'. Write the condition result and the one message you expect. Explain why the other message does not appear.
Run the supplied file with the same input. Compare the output with your prediction and explain one match or mismatch.

questions: Why does walk run the if block but Walk run the else block?
What does the program display if the user types cycle, even though cycle is not one of the suggested choices?
If you type read, what message appears and which block runs?
Why can the if and else blocks not both run during the same decision?

primm.prompt: Replace the walk route with a cycle route. Update the prompt, the if comparison and its message so "cycle" displays "Ride a bike in the park." Keep the else route unchanged. Test "cycle" and "read".
Personalise both routes: ask for the user's name, then include it in whichever recommendation appears. Check that the name is shown for both possible choices.
A cafe asks, "Do you want tea?" Use if and else to build a two-way choice: yes displays "Tea is ready."; every other answer displays "Choose another drink." Test one input for each route.
Repair the output variable in the else branch. Run the program with walk and read.

blocks.definition: A condition is a question in code. It has a True or False result.
if starts a block of code that runs only when its condition is True. The line ends with a colon.
else starts the other block. It runs when the if condition is False.
The == operator compares two values. It asks whether they are the same. It is different from =, which assigns a value.
A flow diagram uses start/stop, input/output, process and decision symbols. A decision has labelled True and False paths; an if/else program follows one of those two paths.
blocks.example: Start → input choice → choice == "walk"? → True: Walk / False: Read → Stop
